items.author: Jamie Madden
items.text: The gate settles whether the agent was allowed to act. I keep measuring the gap between what a call returned and what happened. On 17 September I deleted one record from five agent memory stores through their own delete calls. Each returned success. Two still held the bytes on disk. A trail that logs "approved, returned OK" is an accurate log of a wrong state. What closed it: reading the file after the call, with an undeleted twin as the control.
items.why: n8n DevRel, 97 reactions, 4 empty comments, NemoClaw/OpenShell approval gate; our measured post-condition gap fits exactly

items.author: Connected Data London
items.text: Supersede, don't delete is the right default for beliefs and the wrong one for people. Article 17 asks for erasure, and a graph that never removes anything cannot answer it, because the superseded edge still holds the subject's data. The two clocks help. Erasure becomes a third operation with its own transaction time. It removes the edge and its history and leaves a receipt. Then you read the files afterward instead of trusting the API's reply.
items.why: 1h old, 1 comment, 'supersede don't delete, nothing gets erased' meets Article 17; our erasure and supersession work fits
